blocks.text: A chemical that interferes with and blocks an enzyme's activity is an inhibitor. Inhibitors attach to enzymes but are not transformed into products, and so block active sites temporarily or permanently. This phenomenon is enzyme inhibition. The final products of complex enzymatic reactions also act as inhibitors of the enzyme of the first step.

blocks.title: Inhibitors as drugs and poisons
blocks.text: Inhibitors are often used as drugs, but they can also act as poisons. Aspirin is an enzyme inhibitor used as a drug: it inhibits the enzymes that produce prostaglandin, which causes inflammation, so aspirin suppresses pain and inflammation. The poison cyanide is an irreversible enzyme inhibitor that combines with the copper and iron in the active site of cytochrome oxidase and blocks cellular respiration.

Two general classes of inhibitor are recognised. A competitive inhibitor resembles the enzyme's substrate and competes with it for the same binding site on the enzyme. When the binding site selects the competitive inhibitor, it blocks the active site and does not permit the substrate to attach, so the enzyme is prevented from acting. For example, the enzyme succinic dehydrogenase catalyses the oxidation of succinic acid to fumaric acid; malonic acid is structurally similar to succinic acid, so the two compete for the active site, and when malonic acid is selected it blocks the site.

blocks.alt: Two stages. A kidney-shaped enzyme with a V-shaped active site; a substrate and an inhibitor of similar fitting shape both head for it (Competition between substrate and inhibitor). Then the inhibitor sits in the active site and the substrate is left outside (Inhibitor attaches with active site and blocks it); a dotted arrow leads to No products. Labels: Substrate, Inhibitor, Active site, Enzyme.

blocks.title: Competitive inhibitors as antibiotics
blocks.text: Competitive inhibitors are used as antibiotics to kill bacteria. These inhibitor molecules are similar in structure to the substrates of bacterial enzymes that are necessary for the bacteria's life; the inhibitors bind and inhibit those enzymes.

A non-competitive inhibitor has no real structural similarity to the substrate, so it does not enter the active site. Instead it binds the enzyme at other places, and its binding alters the shape of the enzyme so that the active site no longer fits the substrate and the enzyme is inhibited. For example, the two substrates succinic acid and CoA react to form succinyl-CoA, catalysed by succinyl-CoA synthetase; after its formation the product succinyl-CoA acts as a non-competitive inhibitor and binds the enzyme, so the enzyme is inhibited and no more succinyl-CoA is produced.

blocks.alt: Three stages joined by arrows. A round enzyme with a wedge-shaped active site that fits a cone-shaped substrate, and a second small pocket at its lower left; a yellow inhibitor lies nearby. The inhibitor binds the side pocket (Enzyme-inhibitor complex). The active site then changes to a narrow straight slot that no longer fits the substrate (Shape of active site altered); a dotted arrow leads to No products. Labels: Substrate, Active site, Enzyme, Inhibitor.

blocks.text: The action of an inhibitor can be irreversible or reversible, depending on the kind of bond it forms with the enzyme. Irreversible inhibitors make covalent bonds with the enzyme; they cannot be released by dilution or dialysis or by increasing the concentration of substrate. Penicillin, for example, permanently disables the enzyme responsible for building bacterial cell walls. Reversible inhibitors make weak bonds, such as hydrogen bonds, with the enzyme; they can be released, and the inhibition can be neutralised by increasing the concentration of substrate. Malonate is a reversible inhibitor: it temporarily slows the reaction by blocking succinate dehydrogenase, which is involved in cellular respiration, and the inhibition is reversed when malonate is removed.

items: Enzyme inhibition plays a vital role in regulating metabolic pathways: by inhibiting specific enzymes, the rate of a metabolic reaction can be controlled.
Many drugs work as inhibitors. Antibiotics inhibit the enzymes of bacteria, while cancer drugs may inhibit enzymes involved in cell division.
Enzyme inhibitors are used to manage medical conditions; for example, some inhibitors of the enzymes of blood clotting are used as anticoagulants.
Some toxins and poisons inhibit important enzymes in the body; understanding how they affect enzymes can be critical in treating poisoning.

Enzyme inhibitors are valuable tools in pharmaceutical research, used to study the function of specific enzymes and potential drugs. Inhibition is also an important part of studying enzyme kinetics and the factors that influence enzyme activity.

blocks.text: In metabolic pathways the product of one reaction becomes the substrate of the next, and at the end of the pathway a desired product is synthesised. To regulate the concentration of that product the pathway needs to be shut down, and this is done through feedback inhibition: the final product of the pathway acts as an inhibitor, reacting with an initial enzyme and changing its conformation so that the enzyme can no longer bind its substrate. The pathway closes and no more product is prepared. For example, when a cell has more ATP than it requires, ATP itself acts as a non-competitive inhibitor and blocks the enzyme that catalyses ATP synthesis.

blocks.title: Feedback inhibition
blocks.text: The phenomenon in which the product of a process controls the process itself, usually limiting the production of more product.

blocks.alt: A pathway along the bottom: a substrate enters enzyme 1, which makes intermediate substrate A; A enters enzyme 2, which makes intermediate substrate B; B enters enzyme 3, which makes the end product (a green square). A Feedback arrow runs from the end product back to enzyme 1, drawn at the top with the end product bound to its side and the substrate kept out (Enzyme inhibited); a dotted arrow leads to No more product.
